title: Cost & Latency of Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Every agent you add and every turn it takes multiplies both tokens and wall-clock time. A five-agent crew running six rounds isn't 5x a single call — the shared context reprocessed each turn makes it far worse. The craft is knowing when the extra agents earn their keep, parallelizing independent work so latency doesn't stack sequentially, and recognizing the many tasks where a single well-equipped agent is cheaper, faster, and just as good.

subtopics.title: Every agent-turn is a full model call
subtopics.explanation: Cost scales with the number of (agent x turn) pairs, because each turn is a complete LLM invocation billed on its input and output tokens. Three agents debating for four rounds is up to twelve calls, not one. Internalizing that agents and turns multiply — not add — is the first step to predicting what a crew will cost before you run it.
subtopics.example:
def estimate_calls(n_agents, n_rounds):
    # worst case: every agent speaks every round
    return n_agents * n_rounds

single = 1
crew = estimate_calls(n_agents=3, n_rounds=4)
print(f"single agent: {single} call")
print(f"3-agent crew, 4 rounds: {crew} calls")
# single agent: 1 call
# 3-agent crew, 4 rounds: 12 calls  <- 12x the invocations

subtopics.title: The hidden multiplier: reprocessing shared context
subtopics.explanation: The real cost isn't just the call count — it's that each agent typically re-reads the growing conversation history as input tokens every turn. As the transcript grows, per-turn input cost climbs, so cost grows super-linearly with rounds, not linearly. This reprocessing effect is why a long multi-agent debate can cost 10-20x a single call rather than the naive Nx you'd expect.
subtopics.example:
def crew_input_tokens(base_ctx, per_turn, n_turns):
    total = 0
    ctx = base_ctx
    for _ in range(n_turns):
        total += ctx          # each turn re-reads the whole history
        ctx += per_turn       # history grows every turn
    return total

naive = 500 * 6               # if context never grew
real = crew_input_tokens(base_ctx=500, per_turn=300, n_turns=6)
print(naive, real)  # 3000 7500  -- 2.5x more, and it worsens with length

subtopics.title: Latency stacks sequentially unless you parallelize
subtopics.explanation: If agents take turns, wall-clock latency is the sum of every turn's latency — a six-turn crew feels six times slower than one call. But independent sub-tasks (three searchers hitting three different sources) can run concurrently, so their latency is the max, not the sum. Parallelizing independent work is the single biggest lever for keeping a multi-agent system responsive.
subtopics.example:
import asyncio

async def agent_call(name, seconds):
    await asyncio.sleep(seconds)   # stand-in for model latency
    return f"{name} done"

async def parallel():
    # independent searchers run concurrently -> latency = max, not sum
    return await asyncio.gather(
        agent_call("search_web", 2),
        agent_call("search_docs", 2),
        agent_call("search_db", 2),
    )

results = asyncio.run(parallel())
print(results)   # ~2s total, not 6s

subtopics.title: When the overhead isn't worth it
subtopics.explanation: Multi-agent shines when work genuinely parallelizes or needs distinct expertise (a critic really does catch what a writer misses), but for tasks a single agent can do in one pass, a crew just adds cost, latency, and new failure modes for no accuracy gain. The honest default is a single agent; reach for a crew only when you can name the specific benefit. Choosing the cheaper architecture that meets the quality bar — not the fanciest one — is what separates a production system from a demo.

subtopics.title: Budget every crew with caps and monitoring
subtopics.explanation: Because cost and latency can spiral, production crews carry a token budget, a round cap, and a wall-clock timeout, and they emit per-run metrics (calls, tokens, seconds) so regressions are visible. A crew without a budget is an open-ended bill. Treating cost/latency limits as first-class configuration — not an afterthought — is what makes a multi-agent system safe to run at scale.

foundations.overview: Multi-agent systems trade money and time for capability, and the trade is steeper than it first appears. Every agent turn is a full LLM call billed on tokens, so cost scales with (agents x turns); worse, each turn usually reprocesses the growing shared conversation as input, making cost grow super-linearly with the number of rounds. Latency compounds too: sequential turn-taking sums every turn's latency, so a crew feels as slow as the total of its turns unless you parallelize independent sub-tasks, whose latency is the max rather than the sum. The practical discipline is threefold: default to a single agent and reach for a crew only when the benefit is nameable (genuine parallelism or distinct expertise), parallelize whatever is independent, and put hard caps (tokens, rounds, wall-clock) plus per-run metrics around every crew so an open-ended conversation can never become an open-ended bill.
foundations.formalDefinition: The cost of a multi-agent run is the sum over all agent-turns of (input tokens + output tokens) x price, where per-turn input tokens grow as the shared context accumulates, yielding super-linear growth in rounds. Latency is the sum of turn latencies along the critical path; parallelizing independent turns reduces that path from a sum to a maximum. Budgeting bounds these with token, round, and wall-clock caps.
foundations.whyItMatters: Multi-agent architectures are frequently adopted for prestige rather than need, and the bill and latency arrive later. Understanding that agents and turns multiply cost — and that shared-context reprocessing multiplies it again — lets you predict spend, choose the cheapest architecture that meets the quality bar, and keep systems responsive, which is the difference between an impressive demo and something you can afford to run in production.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of consultants billing by the hour in a meeting. One consultant on a simple question is cheap and fast. Put five in a room and make them talk for six rounds, and you pay all five for all six rounds — and because each must re-read the whole meeting so far to stay in sync, the later rounds cost more than the early ones. If three of them can go research separately at the same time, you get the answers in parallel (max time, one round of pay each) instead of serially — but you should only convene the meeting when the problem actually needs a committee.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Deciding whether a support bot needs a triage-plus-specialist crew or one well-prompted agent, fanning out parallel research agents against independent sources then synthesizing once, setting token and round budgets on a nightly agentic batch job, and profiling a crew's per-run token/latency metrics to find the round where cost blows up.
foundations.performanceImpact: The dominant levers are round count (super-linear via context reprocessing), agent count (linear in calls), and parallelization (turns sum → turns max). Prompt caching of the shared prefix, trimming or summarizing history, capping rounds, and running independent agents concurrently together cut both the token bill and tail latency.

interactiveWidget.title: The multi-agent tax, and how to pay less
interactiveWidget.caption: Where the cost and latency actually come from — and the three levers that control them.

config.note: The seductive mistake with multi-agent systems is arithmetic. 'It's three agents, so maybe three times the cost' — and then the invoice is fifteen times a single call and the response takes twelve seconds. Two multipliers explain the gap. First, calls multiply as (agents x turns): three agents debating four rounds is up to twelve full model calls, each billed on its own input and output tokens. Second, and more insidiously, each turn usually re-reads the entire conversation so far as input tokens. Turn one reads a small context; turn twelve reads everything said in the previous eleven turns. So input cost per turn climbs as the transcript grows, and total cost rises SUPER-linearly with rounds — the tail of a long debate is where the money goes. Latency has the same shape: if agents take strict turns, wall-clock time is the SUM of every turn's latency, so a six-turn crew feels six times slower than one call. Three levers control all of this. LEVER ONE — architecture: default to a single agent, and add a crew only when you can name the payoff (work that genuinely parallelizes, or roles that catch distinct errors like a critic reviewing a writer). For a one-pass task, a crew buys you cost, latency, and new failure modes for no accuracy. LEVER TWO — parallelism: independent sub-tasks (three searchers, three sources) run concurrently, turning a sum of latencies into a max. This is the single biggest responsiveness win and it costs nothing in quality. LEVER THREE — budgets: give every crew a token cap, a round cap, and a wall-clock timeout, and emit per-run metrics (calls, tokens, seconds) so a runaway conversation is a caught exception, not a surprise bill. Add prompt caching of the shared prefix and periodic history trimming and the super-linear curve flattens. The takeaway that saves the most money is also the least glamorous: most tasks do not need a crew, and the ones that do should parallelize and stay on a budget.

checkpoints.prompt: Independent agents run with asyncio.gather, each taking 2 seconds. Roughly how long does the batch take?
checkpoints.code:
import asyncio
async def call(s):
    await asyncio.sleep(s)
async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(call(2), call(2), call(2))
# total wall-clock is approximately ___ seconds
checkpoints.explanation: gather runs the coroutines concurrently, so their latency is the max (~2s), not the sum (6s). Parallelizing independent agent work is the biggest lever for keeping a crew responsive.

checkpoints.prompt: For which task is a multi-agent crew LEAST justified?
options: Research 5 independent sources, then synthesize and critique
Summarize a single document in one pass
A coder drafts and a separate reviewer critiques
Parallel data pulls from three warehouses then merge
checkpoints.explanation: A one-pass summary needs no parallelism and no distinct roles, so a crew only adds cost, latency, and new failure modes. Default to a single agent unless you can name a concrete benefit like parallel work or a distinct reviewing role.

keyTakeaways: Cost scales as (agents x turns), and reprocessing the growing shared context makes it grow super-linearly with rounds.
Sequential turn-taking sums every turn's latency; parallelizing independent sub-tasks makes latency the max, not the sum.
Default to a single agent — add a crew only when you can name the benefit (genuine parallelism or distinct expertise).
Parallelism is the biggest responsiveness lever and costs nothing in quality when sub-tasks are truly independent.
Give every crew token, round, and wall-clock budgets plus per-run metrics so a runaway conversation can't become a runaway bill.
